problem_data.story:
SOFIA'S ALGORITHMS
By A. L. HALEY

Sofia Gupta slumped into the ergonomic chair at her Crestwood Town apartment, her hands trembling as she tried to sort through the latest quarterly reports. She closed her eyes and attempted to breathe deeply, but the twitching in her left eyelid wouldn't stop.

"Just relax, Sofia," her brother Giovanni said from across the room. "You need to take a break from all this stress."

Sofia tried to relax. She really did. But after three minutes of sitting still, she leaped up and began pacing frantically around the living room.

"Sofia!" Giovanni was exasperated now. "Dr. Martinez said you need to step away from work or you're going to have a complete breakdown. Why won't you listen?"

Sofia glared at him. "Martinez! That overpaid quack! I've spent thousands on his consultations. I haven't had a decent night's sleep in months. My hands shake constantly. And what does he prescribe? Meditation apps and breathing exercises! Why, I should send him a bill for wasting my time!" She collapsed back into the chair, her anger barely contained.

"Now, Sofia, you know you've never followed his advice. He told you last year that you'd have to delegate more. Why do you insist on micromanaging every project? It's the strain of trying to control everything that's causing your problems. He told you to take a sabbatical or you'd burn out. Don't blame him for your own stubbornness."

Sofia snorted. "Sabbatical! Sitting on a beach somewhere or hiking through forests! Fine activities for someone who doesn't care about innovation management! And let me correct you. It isn't work stress that's driving me crazy. It's the strain of trying to get some basic competence from the people I have to hire! It's the incompetence of the workforce that's got me beaten! It's the—"

"Hey, Sofia!" Giovanni, scrolling through his tablet, had paused at an article. "Isn't this about those ecosystem restoration stations in Elmwood, Nordavia? The ones you invested in when you were fresh out of university?"

Sofia's hands twitched violently. "Don't mention that disaster!" she rasped. "That deal nearly bankrupted me! The bacterial cultures we developed produced the most unpredictable compounds ever synthesized! My very first investment after graduating, and it almost ended my career before it began!"

Giovanni, whose calm academic demeanor was the complete opposite of Sofia's high-strung entrepreneurial intensity, looked at her over his reading glasses. Sofia's nervous condition was beginning to concern him deeply.

"You're way behind the times, Sofia," he declared. "Don't you know that those compounds have proved to be the most revolutionary biotechnology breakthrough in decades? Don't you know that a consortium has built the largest wellness center in the northern hemisphere there, and that people are traveling from around the world to benefit from the treatments? Sofia, you missed an enormous opportunity!"

Snatching the tablet from Giovanni's hands, Sofia stared at the article which depicted a crystalline structure nestled among restored forests in Elmwood. The main facility was a towering edifice of smart glass that changed colors with the seasons. Between its wings, biodomes housed carefully cultivated ecosystems and treatment centers that looked pristine and inviting in the photographs. A caption noted the facility's recent expansion had attracted record visitors in the past two years.

"Why, I remember now!" exclaimed Giovanni. "That's where the Pattersons went! He was completely burned out and she looked exhausted. They came back completely rejuvenated. Don't you remember? It was just two years ago—they couldn't stop talking about it!"

Giovanni nodded and elaborated on the transformation the Elmwood facility had effected in the Pattersons. "The new treatment wing they built two years ago is supposed to be remarkable. It's perfect for you, Sofia," he advised. "You'd get proper rest during the journey. The new maglev trains have these meditation pods that help you decompress during the trip. And you can evaluate the business potential while you're there recovering. And not only that." He leaned toward his sister confidingly. "The researchers at Chen Biotech have just isolated an enzyme from the Elmwood bacterial cultures that can break down plastic waste into reusable polymers without chemical processing. There's a fortune waiting for the person who secures the licensing rights and learns to scale the production!"

Giovanni had calculated correctly. The tablet lowered in Sofia's hands, and her sharp eyes became shrewd and calculating. She even forgot to twitch. "Maybe you're right, Giovanni," she acknowledged. "Combine recovery with business opportunity, right? After two decades in this industry, I've learned to recognize when multiple interests align."

Looking back at the article, she saw the line about the AI systems. "—the only wellness center managed entirely by artificial intelligence systems—"

"AI systems!" she shrieked. "You mean they've developed them to that level? Why hasn't somebody told me? I'll have Peterson's job! I'll restructure the entire division! I'll—"

"Sofia!" exploded Giovanni. "Stop it! Maybe Peterson doesn't know anything about it! If it's something at the Elmwood Renewal Center, why don't you just go and investigate yourself instead of having a meltdown? That's the only sensible approach!"

"You're right, Giovanni," agreed Sofia decisively. "I'll go and investigate myself. Immediately!" Grabbing her coat, she left at her usual frantic pace.

"Well!" remarked her brother. "All I can say is that they'd better have those meditation pods working perfectly for Sofia's trip!"

The journey to Elmwood did Sofia considerable good. In the meditation pod of the maglev train, she actually relaxed for the first time in years, sinking into a peaceful state with binaural beats and guided visualization that made the eight-hour trip feel like minutes.

It seemed hardly any time at all until they were arriving at the Elmwood station. And then Sofia was stepping onto the platform with unusual calmness still affecting her normally frantic demeanor. She made her way to the transport hub and found herself whisked by automated vehicle directly to the Elmwood Renewal Center.

Appreciatively she gazed around at the vast lobby with its living walls of restored native plants, illuminated by natural light filtering through the smart glass, and at the views of beautiful biodomes framed by a dozen archways. A commemorative plaque near the entrance caught her eye: "Celebrating Two Decades of Renewal—Original Restoration Stations Est. 2024." She remembered that year all too well—fresh out of university, barely twenty-two, convinced she'd found the investment that would make her fortune. Instead, she'd nearly lost everything.

But most of all, the AI systems won her delighted approval.

She could see at once that they had been developed to a remarkably sophisticated level. How, she wondered again, had this been accomplished without her knowledge? Was Giovanni right? Was she losing her edge? Gnawing at the doubt, she watched the AI-controlled service units moving efficiently about, assisting visitors in wheelchairs, delivering meals, guiding newcomers, performing maintenance tasks tirelessly, promptly, and best of all, silently.

Sofia was enthralled. She'd implement them in her company. Regardless of cost! There'd be no more of that frustrating human error and interpersonal conflict that plagued even the best-trained teams! She'd investigate and determine the exact capabilities of these systems while here, and then return home and introduce them into the corporate environment. She'd show them whether she was losing her edge! Briskly she approached the reception desk.

She was immediately confronted with a sample of that human unpredictability that was slowly driving her mad. Machines, she sighed to herself. Wonderful efficient machines! For a woman was arguing loudly with the desk attendant who, poor soul, was a stressed fellow human instead of an AI system. Sofia watched him shrinking and turning pale under the verbal assault.

"A human therapist!" shouted the woman. "I want a real person! For what you charge, you should be able to provide whatever I request! I won't have another of those soulless AI systems managing my treatment, do you hear?"

Everyone within the confines of the huge lobby could hear. The attendant flinched visibly. "Now, Ms. Wyatt," he soothed. "You know the center operates entirely with AI systems. They're much more expensive to develop and maintain than human staff, but so much more precise and consistent. Admit it, they provide excellent service, don't they?"

"That's exactly the problem!" Elena Wyatt glared. "The service is too perfect. I might as well be interacting with a vending machine. I want someone who can understand nuance! I want to be able to express myself without everything being so rigidly programmed!"

Sofia snorted. "Wants someone she can manipulate," she diagnosed. "Someone she can get satisfaction from arguing with." With vast contempt she stepped to the desk beside Elena and sharply tapped for attention.

"One moment, please," begged the harassed attendant. "Just one moment." He turned back to Elena.

But she had turned her glare on Sofia. "You could at least have the courtesy to wait your turn!"

Sofia smirked. "My good woman, I'm not an AI. AI systems, of course, are always courteous. But you should know by now that courtesy isn't always a human strong suit." Leaving Elena temporarily speechless, she beckoned authoritatively to the attendant.

"I've just arrived and need to check in. I'm here for a standard wellness program, no intensive treatments. You can process my registration before continuing your discussion with this lady."

The attendant sputtered. Elena sputtered. But not for nothing was Sofia one of the leading tech entrepreneurs in the region. Sofia's implacable stare won the point. Wiping perspiration from his forehead, the attendant fumbled for a tablet, entered her information, and was about to confirm it when a fist hit the desk with a resounding bang and another voice, male, boomed out at Sofia's elbow.

"This is ridiculous!" roared the voice. "A person could age ten years waiting for service here. Efficiency!" Again his fist struck the counter.

The attendant jumped. He nearly dropped the tablet. Absently holding it, he straightened up to face Elena and the angry newcomer. Hastily he handed Sofia a room card.

"Here you are, Ms. Gupta. I'm sure you'll find it comfortable." With a strained smile he pressed a button and assigned her to the care of a silent and efficient AI guide unit.

The room was more than comfortable. It was stunning. Its panoramic windows framed breathtaking views of the restored Elmwood forests where, Sofia fondly thought, bacterial cultures were busy producing enzymes that would be worth millions to whoever controlled their production rights. A framed photograph on the wall showed the barren landscape from two decades prior—before the restoration stations had transformed it. There remained only the minor challenge of determining how to extract the enzymes economically and to process them in this remote location. Details for her talented research team; mere details...

Leaving her luggage to be handled by the AI system, she went up to the rooftop garden restaurant. Dining boldly on grilled salmon with soup, salad and a light parfait, she gazed out at the restored wilderness, watching birds that had returned to the area after decades of absence. The waiter mentioned that the observation deck—added just two years ago during the expansion—offered even better views. Leaning back in her chair, she even boldly ordered coffee—her first in months—and sipped it happily. For once Giovanni had been absolutely right, she reflected. Yes, Giovanni had hit the mark, and she wouldn't forget it. With a wonderful sense of wellbeing she returned to her room and prepared to rest.

Sofia opened her eyes. Two AI medical units were positioned beside her bed. She saw that they were equipped with diagnostic sensors and treatment apparatus. But she had no further opportunity to examine them. With brisk, perfectly coordinated movements they deployed a transport bed alongside her couch, administered a mild sedative through an arm patch, transferred her onto the bed and began moving her out.

Sofia's voice finally worked. "What's happening?" she demanded. "There's nothing wrong with me. Stop this!"

She struggled to rise, but a mechanical arm gently but firmly held her in place. Inexorably it kept her horizontal.

"You've made an error!" yelled Sofia. "Stop!" But the sedative began taking effect. Her protests became weaker and drowsier. Hazily, as she drifted off, she thought of Elena Wyatt. Maybe the woman had a point, after all.

There was a tentative knock on the door. "Come in," called Sofia bleakly. As soon as the door opened she regretted her invitation, for the opening revealed the large disheveled man who had noisily pounded on the desk demanding service while she was being registered.

"Excuse me," he said hoarsely, "you haven't seen any of those AI units around here, have you?"

Sofia scowled. "Oh, haven't I?" she grated. "AI systems! Do you know what they did to me?" Indignation blazed in her eyes. "Came in while I was resting peacefully after the first proper meal I've enjoyed in months, transported me to the medical wing, and pumped me full of supplements and ran diagnostics! The only peace I've had in months!" Darkly she sank her chin onto her fist and contemplated the outrage.

"Why didn't you stop them?" reasonably asked the visitor.

"Stop an AI system?" Sofia glared. "How? You can't reason with the things. And as for physical intervention—it's human against machine. You try it!" She ground her teeth together in futile rage. "And to think I had the absurd notion that AI systems were the solution to everything! Why, I was ready to implement them throughout my entire company!"

The big man placed his large hands on his own substantial stomach and groaned. "I'm genuinely sorry it was you and not me. I could use some of that intervention right now. Must have been that heavy meal I ate after all that processed food I've been consuming."

"Processed food?" A faint spark of alertness pierced Sofia's dull rage. "You mean you work out here in the production facilities?"

"That's right. How'd you guess? I'm George Edwards, superintendent of one of the enzyme extraction plants. Been working the original sites since they started operations—feels like a lifetime ago. Good pay, but what a job! Isolated location. Climate-controlled facilities. Hazmat protocols. Prefab housing. Synthetic nutrition. Nothing else. Just nothing. That's where they could really use AI systems. It's certainly no environment for people long-term. And in fact, there aren't many people left there. If old Melissa Chen only knew it, her operation is about to collapse."

Sofia sat up as if electrified. She opened her mouth to speak. But just then the door opened efficiently and two AI units entered. With a horrified stare, Sofia clutched her stomach. She saw a third unit enter, maneuvering a mobility chair.

"A wheelchair!" squeaked Sofia. "I tell you, there's nothing wrong with me! Take it away! I'm only here for standard wellness! Believe me! Take it away!"

The AI units ignored her. For the first time in her spectacular and aggressive career Sofia was confronting entities that she could neither negotiate with, intimidate, charm nor dismiss. It shattered her remaining confidence. She began waving her hands helplessly.

The AI units not only ignored Sofia. They paid no attention at all to George Edwards, who was tugging at their mechanical frames pleading, "Take me instead. I genuinely need treatment. I need all the help I can get. Take me! I'm falling apart here—"

Impassively they lifted Sofia up, placed her in the chair, secured her safely and proceeded out with her.

Dejectedly George returned to his own room. Again he tried the room's communication system; but as usual an AI voice responded pleasantly, mechanically, and unhelpfully. He disconnected and went miserably to bed.

There was something nagging at Sofia's mind. Something she should address. Something that concerned AI systems. But she was too exhausted to work it out.

For five days now these AI systems had subjected her to an ordeal that made her flinch every time she thought about it. Which wasn't often, since she was almost beyond thinking. They immersed her in mineral baths and kept her there until she was thoroughly treated. They had her breathe therapeutic compounds until she felt dizzy. They brought her strange nutritional preparations and monitored her until she consumed them. They administered treatments and exercises and therapies.

Whenever they left her alone, she simply collapsed into bed and slept. There was nothing else to do anyway. They'd taken her clothes; and the communication system, after an announcement that she would have limited access for two weeks, gave her nothing but automated responses.

"Persecution, that's what this is!" she moaned desperately. And she turned away from the mirror, which showed her that she was beginning to look healthy instead of the pale gray to which she had become accustomed. She closed her mind to the fact that she was sleeping soundly for hours like she hadn't in years, and that she was developing such an appetite that she could almost enjoy even those strange breakfast preparations they provided. She was determined to be furious. As soon as she could stay awake long enough to be.

She hadn't been awake long this time before George Edwards was there again, still complaining about his lack of treatments. "Nothing yet," he gloomily informed Sofia. "They haven't touched me. I just can't understand it. After I registered for the full program and paid in advance! And I can't find any way out of this section. The other rooms are empty and the elevator doesn't have manual controls. The AI units have to come and retrieve you or you're trapped."

"Trapped!" snarled Sofia. "I'm never trapped! And I refuse to wait any longer to escape this—this prison! Listen, George. I've been thinking. Or trying to, with what's left of my brain. You arrived just when that incompetent attendant was registering me. I'll bet that attendant got confused and gave me the wrong room assignment. I'll bet you're supposed to have this room and I'm receiving your treatments. Why don't we switch rooms and see what happens?"

"Say, maybe you're right!" George's eyes gleamed with hope. "I'll get my things."

Sofia's eyebrows rose. "You mean they left you your clothes?"

"Why, yes. You mean they took yours?"

Sofia nodded. An idea began forming. "Leave your things, would you? I'm desperate! I'm going to see the director of this nightmare if I have to go down wrapped in a bedsheet. Your clothes would be better than that."

George, looking over Sofia's slight frame, grunted doubtfully. "Maybe you could make them work somehow. Roll up everything. It's fine with me, but just don't lose anything when you're down there in that fancy lobby."

Sofia looked at her watch. "Time to go. Relax. The AI units will arrive any minute now. If you're the only person in the room, I'm confident they'll take you. They aren't programmed to figure it out. And don't worry about me. I'll manage your clothes."

Sofia had guessed correctly. Gleefully from the doorway of her new room she watched the AI units transport her equally delighted neighbor for his first treatment. Then she closed the door and began putting on George's clothing.

The result was absurd. She looked like a child in adult clothes, except for the remarkably tired and gaunt face emerging from a collar several sizes too large. And she was barefoot. She was completely unable to walk in George's enormous shoes. But Sofia was a determined woman. She didn't even flinch at her reflection. Firmly she stepped over to George's communication panel. "This is room 618," she said authoritatively. "Send the elevator for me. I need to go down to the lobby."

She'd guessed correctly again. "It will arrive shortly, Ms. Gupta," responded the AI operator. Hopefully she stepped out into the corridor and shuffled to the elevator.

Only the AI units were immune to Sofia Gupta's progress across the elegant lobby.

She was an anomaly in its refined beauty, a bizarre sight that froze the other visitors into staring clusters. Stepping out of the elevator, she had charted a course for the reception desk which stood like an island in the vast space, and now she shuffled determinedly toward it, ignoring the oversized trousers dragging around her bare feet. Only the AI units maintained their composure.

The attendant was the first to recover from the collective shock. Frantically he pressed the button that would summon the AI security units. With a gasp of relief he saw the two substantial mechanical units moving steadily forward. He pointed to Sofia. "Retrieve that guest!" he ordered. "Take her to the—to the treatment wing!"

"Absolutely not!" yelled Sofia. "I want to see the director!" Nimbly she circled the security units and leaped behind the desk. She began throwing things at the AI units. Things like tablets and input devices and filing systems. Especially, filing systems.

"Stop it!" begged the attendant. "You'll destroy the database! We'll never recover it! Stop it!"

"Call them off!" snarled Sofia. "Call them off or I'll wreck your entire system!" She put a hand on the main control panel and prepared to shut it down.

With one last appalled look at the madwoman, the attendant grabbed a control device and pointed it at the approaching AI units. They became suddenly motionless.

"That's better!" Sofia straightened up and meticulously smoothed the collar of her enormous coat. "Now—the director, please."

"This—this way, please." With reluctant steps the attendant led Sofia across the width of the lobby among the fascinated guests. He was beyond words. Opening the discreet door, he gestured Sofia inside and returned doggedly to his desk, where he began retrieving scattered items and simultaneously composing his resignation in his mind.

Brushing aside the startled assistant in the outer office, Sofia shuffled and flapped straight into the inner office. The director, who was busy reviewing reports behind her sleek desk, jerked upright and stared at the intruder. "Excuse me—" she began.

"Don't 'excuse me' me!" snapped Sofia. She glared back at the director. Reaching as far across the desktop as she could stretch, she shook her small fist. "Do you know who I am? I'm Sofia Gupta, of Gupta Technologies! And do you know why I don't even have identification to prove it? Do you know why I have to make my way downstairs in clothing that makes me look ridiculous? Do you know why? Because that incompetent attendant of yours assigned me the wrong room and those infernal AI systems of yours then proceeded to imprison me! Me, Sofia Gupta! Why, I'll sue you until you'll be fortunate if you have a single server left in this automated asylum!"

Leah Ford, the director, paled. Then she began to flush in an alarming pattern. And suddenly with a heavy sigh, she collapsed into her chair. With a shaking hand she wiped her forehead. "My AI systems!" she muttered. "As if I designed the damned things!"

Despondently she looked at Sofia. "Go ahead and sue, Ms. Gupta. If you don't, somebody else will. And if nobody sues, we'll fail anyway, at the rate our guest retention is declining. I'm ready to submit my resignation."

Again she sighed. "The problem," she explained, "is that those AI systems are completely logical and rule-based, and people aren't. There's no way to reconcile the two. It's volatile. Maybe people can gradually adapt to AI systems, but they haven't yet. Only we had to discover it the hard way. We—" she grimaced with disgust—"had to pioneer in AI integration. And it cost us so much that we can't afford to convert back to human staff. So—Operation AI is about to bankrupt the consortium."

Listening, an unexpected calm settled on Sofia. Thoughtfully now she hooked a chair to the desk with her bare foot, sat down and reached for the water glass that Leah automatically offered her. "Oh, I don't know," she said mildly.

Leah leaned forward like someone grasping at hope. "What do you mean, you don't know? You're threatening to sue us into oblivion, aren't you?"

Carefully Sofia sipped the water. "It seems to me that these AI systems might be useful in quite a different capacity. I might even negotiate with your consortium to acquire them—at a reasonable price, naturally—and forget the grievances I've suffered at your establishment."

Leah leaned toward her incredulously. "You mean you want these AI systems after what you've seen and experienced?"

Calmly Sofia set down the glass. "Of course, you'd have to consider that it would be experimental for me as well. And there's the lawsuit I'm clearly entitled to file. However, I'm willing to discuss the matter with your board."

With hope emerging for the first time in weeks, Leah lifted her head. "Ms. Gupta, to be rid of these problematic AI systems, I'll support you completely! I'll notify the board immediately. Immediately, Ms. Gupta! And while we wait for them, allow me to offer you proper accommodations as a guest of the center." Coming around to Sofia, she warmly shook Sofia's small hand, and then personally escorted her not merely to the door but across the lobby to the elevator.

Sofia gazed out at the stunned audience. This was more like the treatment she was accustomed to! Proudly she squared her thin shoulders inside the massive jacket and stepped into the elevator. She was ready for the second phase of her private Operation AI.

Back in Crestwood Town it was a warm, clear autumn day—the kind of day that made the city sparkle. Giovanni and his wife waited eagerly while the maglev train docked and the passengers disembarked.

"Look, Giovanni!" His wife clutched his arm. "The doors are opening."

They watched the doors slide open and the passengers emerge, looking refreshed from their journey.

"There she is!" cried Giovanni. "Doesn't she look wonderful! It's amazing! Look at her!"

And indeed, Sofia was stepping briskly forward, looking energetic and healthy and years younger. She came across to them actually smiling. It was the first genuine smile they had seen on her face in years.

"Well, you did it again!" exclaimed Giovanni warmly. "So you pulled off another deal!"

Sofia grinned. "Yes, I executed a very favorable transaction. I acquired Chen Biotech's enzyme operation and staffed the facility with the center's AI systems. Got both at excellent prices. Both operations were failing because they didn't have the sense to exchange their resources. Feel I owe you something for that tip about enzymes, Giovanni, so I've allocated some equity to you. Acceptable?"

"Acceptable?" Giovanni gulped. Why, his high-strung sister was showing gratitude after all. "Acceptable! Absolutely! But aren't you going to use some of those AI systems for your company? Aren't they efficient and all that?"

Sofia's smile vanished. "Don't even suggest such a thing!" she yelped. "You don't know what you're saying! I lived with those things for weeks. I wouldn't have one in the office! Keep them in the factory where they belong!"

She glimpsed the composed, wonderfully human face of her assistant, waiting patiently in the background. "Oh there you are, Eric." She turned to her brother. "Busy day ahead. See you later—"

"Same old Sofia," observed Giovanni. Then he thought of the equity. "What say we celebrate our stake in the venture?"

"Wonderful!" His wife squeezed his arm, and smiling at each other, they left the station.
